videos.title: The Nervous System, Part 1
videos.watchFor: Separate sensory input, central processing, and motor output, then connect that pathway to the unit's neuron and sensory evidence.
videos.localFallback: The nervous system detects change, integrates information in the CNS, and coordinates responses through peripheral pathways. For unit review, connect that route to neuron signalling, synapses, reflexes, and sensory receptors.

videos.title: Structure of a Neuron
videos.watchFor: Connect each neuron structure to the direction of information flow.
videos.localFallback: Dendrites receive input, the cell body integrates it, the axon carries an action potential, and terminals communicate with the next cell.

videos.title: Reflex Arc
videos.watchFor: Track the route from receptor to spinal integration and motor response.
videos.localFallback: A withdrawal reflex can use a receptor, sensory neuron, spinal interneuron, motor neuron, and effector before conscious pain is processed.

videos.title: Types of Neurons: Reflex Arcs
videos.watchFor: Distinguish sensory, interneuron, and motor roles in one complete pathway.
videos.localFallback: Sensory neurons carry input toward the CNS, interneurons integrate within the CNS, and motor neurons carry output to effectors.

videos.title: Action Potential Explained
videos.watchFor: Match channel state and ion direction to each voltage phase.
videos.localFallback: Threshold opens voltage-gated sodium channels, sodium entry depolarizes the membrane, sodium-channel inactivation and potassium efflux repolarize it, and channel recovery creates the refractory period.

videos.title: Action Potential in the Neuron
videos.watchFor: Pause at each graph phase and name the open channel, moving ion, and voltage direction.
videos.localFallback: An action potential is an all-or-none, regenerated voltage event. Sodium entry drives depolarization; sodium-channel inactivation and potassium exit drive repolarization; delayed potassium-channel closing contributes to the undershoot.

videos.watchFor: Notice what threshold changes about voltage-gated sodium channels.
videos.localFallback: A subthreshold change fades, but threshold recruits enough voltage-gated sodium channels to start regenerative depolarization.

videos.title: Action Potential, Part 2
videos.watchFor: Connect sodium-channel inactivation and potassium-channel timing to recovery.
videos.localFallback: The falling phase is produced by sodium-channel inactivation and delayed potassium efflux, not by a sudden reversal of the sodium-potassium pump.

videos.title: Excitatory vs. Inhibitory Neurotransmitters
videos.watchFor: Compare how synaptic input moves membrane potential toward or away from threshold.
videos.localFallback: Excitatory input usually moves the postsynaptic membrane toward threshold; inhibitory input moves it away. A neuron integrates many inputs rather than obeying one transmitter in isolation.

videos.title: Synaptic Transmission
videos.watchFor: Not learner-delivered.
videos.localFallback: The local lesson fully sequences neurotransmitter release, receptor binding, signal ending, and common sites of disruption.
videos.exclusionReason: The source video is unavailable through the provider.

videos.title: Synaptic Transmission
videos.watchFor: Follow the sequence from arriving action potential to postsynaptic response.
videos.localFallback: An arriving action potential opens calcium channels, vesicles release transmitter, transmitter binds receptors, the postsynaptic cell changes, and clearance mechanisms end the signal.

videos.title: Peripheral Nervous System
videos.watchFor: Organize somatic and autonomic pathways beneath the PNS.
videos.localFallback: The PNS links receptors and effectors to the CNS. Somatic pathways serve skeletal muscle; autonomic pathways regulate smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands.

videos.title: Peripheral Nervous System
videos.watchFor: Not learner-delivered.
videos.localFallback: The local nervous-system hierarchy provides the complete required explanation.
videos.exclusionReason: The source video is not available for reliable embedded playback.

videos.title: The Autonomic Nervous System
videos.watchFor: Compare sympathetic and parasympathetic effects organ by organ rather than as universal on/off states.
videos.localFallback: Autonomic branches often have opposing effects, but their actions are tissue-specific and coordinated with the body situation.

videos.title: The Fight, Flight, Freeze Response
videos.watchFor: Not learner-delivered.
videos.localFallback: The local lesson distinguishes rapid sympathetic-adrenal responses from slower endocrine support without self-diagnosis.
videos.exclusionReason: Medical self-help framing is not needed for this curriculum outcome.

videos.title: Turn Off Anxiety in Your Nervous System
videos.watchFor: Not learner-delivered.
videos.localFallback: The course teaches stress physiology but does not provide individual medical or mental-health treatment advice.
videos.exclusionReason: Medical self-help framing duplicates the local stress instruction.

videos.title: Central Nervous System
videos.watchFor: Connect each major brain or spinal structure to evidence, not personality labels.
videos.localFallback: The brain and spinal cord integrate information through distributed networks; symptoms can suggest a location but do not establish a diagnosis.

videos.title: The Human Brain: Major Structures and Functions
videos.watchFor: Identify how named regions work as connected networks.
videos.localFallback: Major regions have characteristic functions, but complex behaviour emerges from interacting brain networks rather than one isolated centre.

videos.title: Anatomy of the Brain
videos.watchFor: Use location and connections to distinguish cerebrum, cerebellum, brainstem, and diencephalon.
videos.localFallback: The brain model in Lesson 6 connects major regions to coordination, sensation, movement, language, memory, and homeostatic regulation.

videos.exclusionReason: The topic is outside the Unit A instructional focus.

videos.title: Understanding Addiction as a Disease
videos.watchFor: Not learner-delivered.
videos.localFallback: Lesson 5 addresses synaptic drug effects without extending into an unrelated addiction unit.
videos.exclusionReason: The topic is outside the Unit A instructional focus.

videos.title: Nervous System
videos.watchFor: Use the review to rebuild the path from receptor to CNS integration to response.
videos.localFallback: For nervous-system review, connect neuron signalling, synapses, CNS/PNS organization, reflexes, and sensory pathways as one information-control system.
videos.exclusionReason: The source video is no longer available for reliable embedded playback.

videos.title: Vision
videos.watchFor: Separate optical focusing, retinal transduction, and brain processing.
videos.localFallback: Cornea and lens focus light; photoreceptors change signalling in response to light; retinal circuits process the pattern; ganglion-cell axons carry output through the optic nerve to central visual pathways.

videos.title: What Is Night Blindness?
videos.watchFor: Connect rod function and vitamin A to evidence while avoiding self-diagnosis.
videos.localFallback: Rods support dim-light vision and use retinal derived from vitamin A, but difficulty seeing at night has multiple possible causes that require clinical assessment.

videos.title: Anatomy of the Eye
videos.watchFor: Trace light through transparent structures to the retina.
videos.localFallback: Light passes through cornea, aqueous humour, pupil, lens, and vitreous humour before reaching the retina; optic-nerve output is already neural information.

videos.title: Hearing and Balance
videos.watchFor: Track the change from pressure wave to mechanical vibration to hair-cell signalling.
videos.localFallback: The outer and middle ear transmit vibration; cochlear fluid movement bends hair cells; the vestibular apparatus uses related mechanoreceptors to detect head motion and position.

videos.title: How Hearing Works
videos.watchFor: Name the energy form at each step of the hearing pathway.
videos.localFallback: Sound pressure moves the eardrum and ossicles, creates fluid waves in the cochlea, bends hair cells, and produces neural signals.

videos.title: The Science of Hearing
videos.watchFor: Notice how the cochlea separates frequency information.
videos.localFallback: Different cochlear regions respond most strongly to different frequencies, creating an organized neural representation of sound.

videos.title: Human Ear: Structure and Working
videos.watchFor: Trace the pathway without treating an online tone as a hearing test.
videos.localFallback: The lesson provides a labelled ear pathway and a synthetic audiogram; no high-volume or diagnostic audio activity is required.

videos.title: The Vestibular System
videos.watchFor: Distinguish rotational from linear acceleration and head orientation.
videos.localFallback: Semicircular canals detect rotation; the utricle and saccule respond to linear acceleration and head orientation relative to gravity.

videos.title: Endocrine System, Part 1
videos.watchFor: Compare hormone transport and target-cell response with neural signalling.
videos.localFallback: Endocrine glands release hormones into blood; only cells with compatible receptors and response machinery react.

videos.watchFor: Not learner-delivered.
videos.localFallback: Study strategy is outside the course media collection.
videos.exclusionReason: The study-skills topic is outside the Unit A instructional focus.

videos.title: Thyroid Gland and Thyroid Problems
videos.watchFor: Trace TRH, TSH, thyroid hormone, targets, and feedback separately.
videos.localFallback: Thyroid hormone changes metabolism and development; hypothalamic and pituitary signals regulate release through negative feedback.

videos.title: Insulin and Glucagon
videos.watchFor: Compare the high-glucose and low-glucose branches, then identify which target is tissue-specific.
videos.localFallback: After glucose rises, beta cells increase insulin release and target tissues change uptake, storage, and production. When glucose falls, alpha cells increase glucagon and the liver increases glucose output. Not every tissue responds to insulin in the same way.

videos.title: Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes
videos.watchFor: Separate beta-cell loss from reduced insulin responsiveness and avoid single-cause claims.
videos.localFallback: Type 1 diabetes involves autoimmune beta-cell destruction. Type 2 diabetes is multifactorial and can involve reduced insulin responsiveness and impaired secretion; treatment is individualized.

videos.title: Adrenal Stress: Short Term and Long Term
videos.watchFor: Not learner-delivered.
videos.localFallback: A higher-authority, curriculum-focused stress resource is used instead.
videos.exclusionReason: A lower-authority duplicate is replaced by the selected stress resource.

videos.title: What Does Stress Do to Your Body?
videos.watchFor: Distinguish immediate signalling from longer-term physiological effects.
videos.localFallback: Rapid sympathetic and adrenal-medulla responses mobilize resources; longer endocrine responses can alter metabolism, circulation, immune activity, sleep, and cognition.

videos.title: How Stress Affects Your Body
videos.watchFor: Compare short-term adaptive responses with evidence from prolonged stress.
videos.localFallback: A short stress response can support immediate action. Persistent activation can affect metabolism, pressure, sleep, immune activity, and cognition; individual health advice belongs with qualified care.

videos.title: The Pituitary Gland
videos.watchFor: Separate hypothalamic control, anterior-pituitary secretion, and posterior-pituitary release.
videos.localFallback: The hypothalamus regulates the anterior pituitary and produces ADH and oxytocin released by the posterior pituitary; the pituitary works within feedback axes rather than acting alone.

videos.title: The Anterior Pituitary
videos.watchFor: Trace one releasing hormone, pituitary hormone, target gland, and feedback signal.
videos.localFallback: Anterior-pituitary axes connect hypothalamic signals to downstream glands and are regulated by feedback from target-gland hormones.

videos.title: Endocrine System, Part 2
videos.watchFor: Rebuild one complete hormone cascade and identify where feedback returns.
videos.localFallback: For endocrine review, trace stimulus, control centre, gland, hormone, receptor-bearing target, response, and feedback evidence as separate steps.

videos.title: Endocrine System: Stress Hormones
videos.watchFor: Compare adrenal-medulla and adrenal-cortex signals by timing and effect.
videos.localFallback: Epinephrine supports rapid responses; cortisol and aldosterone have different slower targets and regulatory pathways.

videos.title: Endocrine System: Blood Glucose Hormones
videos.watchFor: Identify the initiating change and the response that opposes it.
videos.localFallback: Insulin-linked and glucagon-linked pathways form two feedback branches that oppose rises and falls in blood glucose.

videos.title: Endocrine System: Growth and Metabolism Hormones
videos.watchFor: Keep growth-hormone and thyroid-hormone axes distinct.
videos.localFallback: Growth-hormone and thyroid axes both affect growth or metabolism but use different pituitary signals, targets, and feedback evidence.
